parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from verbs, especially expressing that something can, may, or is suitable to undergo the specif…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German -bar (“originally bearing; adjective-forming suffix”), from Old Saxon -bāri (“bearing, having; characterized by”), from Proto-Germanic *bēriz (“bearing, carrying”). Ultimately related to bære (“to bear, carry”) and bær (“pregnant or having recently calved, of a cow”).

parole.significato: Suffix giving an adjective a nounal meaning; -ness -ity.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German -hēt, -heit, from Old Saxon -hēd, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz (“manner, way; state”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keyt-, *(s)keydʰ- (“clear, bright, shining”). Cognate with Danish -hed, Swedish -het, German -heit, Dutch -heid and English -hood.

parole.significato: an ancestor; ancestry (deceased relative a good distance back in time)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ane, an, from Proto-Germanic *anô (“male ancestor; forefather”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“on, onto”). Cognate with German Ahn, Latin anus, Yiddish אָן (on), Danish ane and possibly Icelandic ái.
Borrowed from Middle Low German arbeit, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz. Compare with Swedish arbete, Danish arbejde, and Faroese arbeiði.
Borrowed from Middle Low German barsch, from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“perch, bass”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórs-o-s, from *bʰers- (“top, tip, point”).

parole.significato: to commend, commit, entrust; to give over, especially to God
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bevalen (“to command, entrust”), equivalent to be- (“be-”) + vēlen (“to hide, conceal, entrust”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *felhaną (“to hide, conceal; entrust”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk befale, befala, Danish befale, Swedish befalla, and German befehlen.

parole.significato: to agree with, suit, or please someone; to have a certain effect on someone's health, condition, or well-being
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bekomen (“to come to something; to get; to come into a certain state”), from Old Saxon bikuman (“to come to, arrive at”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną (“to come to, arrive”). From Middle Low German beswīmen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swīmaną (“to sway, to swoon”).
From Middle Low German blick, bleck, from Proto-Germanic *bliką. Cognate with Dutch blik, German Blech (both “sheet metal”). Related with etymology 1, but not the same word.
From Middle Low German dēl, deil, from Old Saxon dēl, from Proto-Germanic *dailą, *dailiz (“part, portion, deal”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German verwe or varwe, from Proto-Germanic *farwō. Cognate with German Farbe, Danish farve and Swedish färg. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per-, *perḱ- (“motley, coloured”).
From Middle Low German vorlaten, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Compare English forlet, German verlassen, German Low German laten, late. Originally meaning "abandon", "forgive".

parole.significato: to be shipwrecked (of a person at sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vorliesen (“to lose”), from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną, cognate with German verlieren, Dutch verliezen, English forlese (obsolete), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍃𐌰𐌽 (fraliusan).
Borrowed from Middle Low German vrisch, from Old Saxon *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-.

parole.significato: a pole or other piece of wood made for a specific purpose
parole.testo: From Middle Low German of same origin as modern German Holz. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hultą, it is a doublet of holt (Etymology 1).

From Middle Low German kōte, kāte (“hut”), from Proto-Germanic *kutǭ ~ *kutą. Cognate with German Kate. Compare also Norwegian Nynorsk kote, Swedish kåta, which are partially from the same word and partially from Proto-Samic *koatē.

From Middle Low German kunst (“knowledge, ability”), from Old Saxon kunst, from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), from the verb *kunnaną (“to know, recognise”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥néh₃ti (“to know, recognize”), from *ǵneh₃- (“to know”) + *-né- (forms transitive imperfective v
From Middle Low German neren, from Old Saxon nerian, from Proto-Germanic *nazjaną (“to rescue, heal”), causative of *nesaną (“to survive, recover”).
From Middle Low German putze, pusse, posse. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to hit”), likely in part through Old French boce (“bump”). Compare German Posse, Dutch poets.

parole.significato: a rib bone, especially from a slaughtered animal
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ribbe (“rib bone; raised stripe”), also rebbe (“rib bone; raised stripe”), from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib”); some technical senses were later influenced by English rib. Doublet of ribb (“rib, flange; ribbed fabric”) and rev (“reef”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ribbe,

parole.significato: to pluck the feathers from poultry or another bird
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ribben (“to pluck; break hemp”), probably from Proto-Germanic *rippōną (“to tear off”) or *ribōną (“to tear off”), intensive formations beside *rīfaną (“to tear”). Borrowed from Middle Low German roder, from Old Saxon *rōthar, from Proto-Germanic *rōþrą.

parole.significato: a state of intoxication caused by alcohol, narcotics, or another intoxicating substance, often involving reduced inhibi…
parole.testo: Deverbal from ruse (“to rush, charge; to move violently”), probably from Middle Low German rūsen (“to make noise, rumble”). The Low German verb probably belongs to an expressive or onomatopoeic Germanic word family denoting rushing, roaring, or rapid movement, also represented by Middle High German
Borrowed from Middle Low German selschap, from Old Saxon selskepi, from Proto-Germanic *saljaskapiz.
From Middle Low German schen, geschen, cognate with Danish ske, Dutch geschieden, German geschehen and Limburgish sji-jje, from Proto-Germanic *skehaną (“to spring, come up, emerge, happen”).
From Middle Low German [Term?], ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skraudaną. Compare Swedish skrota and Danish skrotte.
From Middle Low German slot, from Proto-Germanic *slutą.
From Middle Low German smak, from Proto-Germanic *smakkuz (“taste, smack”).

parole.significato: a stocking (covering most of the leg)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German strümpe, from Proto-Germanic *strumpaz.

parole.significato: like this, like that, in this way, in that way
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sōdān, a compound of 1. sō (“so”) from Proto-Germanic *swa, and 2. dān (“done”), past participle of dōn (“to do”), from Proto-Germanic *dōną.
From Middle Low German ôven, from Old Saxon ōvian, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną.
